## Proof

We use the arctangent subtraction identity. For $A, B$ with $AB > -1$:

$$\arctan A - \arctan B = \arctan\!\left(\frac{A-B}{1+AB}\right).$$

Set $A = \dfrac{x}{n}$ and $B = \dfrac{x}{n+1}$. Since $AB = \dfrac{x^2}{n(n+1)} > 0 > -1$, the identity applies directly. Compute the argument:

$$\frac{A-B}{1+AB} = \frac{\dfrac{x}{n}-\dfrac{x}{n+1}}{1+\dfrac{x^2}{n(n+1)}} = \frac{\dfrac{x}{n(n+1)}}{\dfrac{n(n+1)+x^2}{n(n+1)}} = \frac{x}{n(n+1)+x^2}.$$

Therefore each summand telescopes:

$$\arctan\!\left(\frac{x}{n(n+1)+x^2}\right) = \arctan\!\left(\frac{x}{n}\right) - \arctan\!\left(\frac{x}{n+1}\right).$$

Summing from $n=1$ to $N$:

$$\sum_{n=1}^{N}\arctan\!\left(\frac{x}{n(n+1)+x^2}\right) = \arctan(x) - \arctan\!\left(\frac{x}{N+1}\right).$$

Taking $N\to\infty$, since $\dfrac{x}{N+1}\to 0$ and $\arctan$ is continuous,

$$f(x) = \lim_{N\to\infty}\left[\arctan(x) - \arctan\!\left(\frac{x}{N+1}\right)\right] = \arctan(x).$$

Hence

$$f'(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2}, \qquad f'(2) = \frac{1}{1+4} = \frac{1}{5}.$$

$$\boxed{f'(2) = \dfrac{1}{5}}$$
